title: Findings of MEGA: Maths Explanation with LLMs using the Socratic Method for Active Learning
venue: IEEE Signal Processing Magazine (special issue: AI for Education)
extended_summary:
This paper asks whether a novel LLM-based mathematics explanation approach called MEGA improves students’ learning experience compared with a traditional chain-of-thought (CoT) explanation style. MEGA combines the Socratic method, chain-of-thought reasoning, simplified gamification with two answer choices, and formative feedback. The authors are primarily interested in whether interactive, stepwise questioning leads to better perceived explanations and better model behavior than standard step-by-step answers.

The intervention was implemented as an online app and evaluated with two benchmark math datasets: GSM8K (treated as easier) and MATH (treated as harder). The participants were university master’s students in a Text Mining course at Luleå University of Technology, Sweden. Students performed blind pairwise comparisons between MEGA and CoT explanations generated by two LLMs that could follow the prompt reliably (GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet). They also provided free-text feedback and reported their usual learning preference. The study further examined model accuracies under MEGA, Socratic sub-steps, and CoT.

The main finding is that students generally preferred MEGA over CoT, especially for harder MATH problems, where MEGA was rated clearly better for understanding. For easier GSM8K items, MEGA was only slightly preferred and some students considered the interaction unnecessary. The paper also reports that the Socratic prompting sometimes improved accuracy but also exposed hallucination and brittleness in the LLMs. Overall, the paper concludes that MEGA can support more engaging and clearer mathematics explanations for difficult problems, but its benefits are less pronounced for easy problems and it does not eliminate model errors.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical comparison, but it is not a K-12 study and uses a human judgment design rather than a strong counterfactual on learner achievement. Evidence is largely qualitative/preference-based with no randomized student learning outcome measure or effect size.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests a potentially useful interactive LLM math-explanation approach, especially for harder problems, but the evidence is on perceived explanation quality rather than demonstrated learning gains. Because there is no direct grades 6–8 ChatGPT mathematics intervention evidence and no measurable achievement effect, impact remains unclear/modest.

interventions.use_case: LLM-driven math explanation system (MEGA) that uses the Socratic method, chain-of-thought prompting, simplified two-option gamification, and formative feedback to explain GSM8K and MATH problems.

finding.finding_summary: This paper does not test a K-12 student learning intervention in grades 6–8; instead, university students evaluated whether MEGA or plain CoT explanations were better for understanding math solutions. Students preferred MEGA more often on harder MATH items (47.5% vs 26.67% for CoT; n=60 sampled problems per dataset), but the paper reports this as a subjective learning-experience preference rather than an achievement gain. Reported accuracy patterns were also mixed: MEGA and Socratic accuracies varied by dataset/difficulty, with accuracies generally dropping at higher MATH difficulty levels; no standardized learning effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Student pairwise preference for explanation quality; LLM solution accuracy on GSM8K and MATH items
finding.study_size: n=34 evaluators; n=60 sampled problems per dataset
finding.confidence_interval: p=0.0201 for MATH preference difference; p=0.6731 for GSM8K

finding.finding_summary: The main non-achievement outcome was perceived understandability/engagement of the explanation method, which the authors link to active learning, critical thinking, and student-centered learning. Students generally judged MEGA as more engaging and easier to follow on harder problems, but also noted that the interactive format could be tedious for easy questions; the paper provides no causal estimate, only preference counts and qualitative comments.
finding.measure: Unanimous student preference for explanation method; free-text feedback on ease of understanding and engagement
finding.study_size: n=34 evaluators; n=120 problem instances total
